extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (guidance also useful to applicants and practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting 35 U.S.C. §101 subject‑matter eligibility analysis under MPEP §2106, including Step 1 (statutory category) and Step 2A (Alice/Mayo first part) determinations. Focused on examiner procedures, tests, examples, and best practices for identifying judicial exceptions and assessing whether claims integrate such exceptions into practical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1 — statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter (i.e., one of the four statutory categories)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate after determining what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing claims under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI). If the claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO), the claim is non‑statutory and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. If the claim falls within one or more statutory categories (Step 1: YES), proceed to determine whether it is eligible at Pathway A or requires further analysis at Step 2A for judicial exceptions. Examples: transitory signals (propagating carrier waves) are non‑statutory even if physical; a machine‑readable medium whose BRI includes carrier waves should be rejected under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) and review of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Before applying eligibility steps, determine what the applicant has invented by reviewing the entire disclosure and construing claims according to the BRI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation at each eligibility step should be made after determining the applicant's invention via whole‑application review and BRI. If the BRI covers non‑statutory embodiments, point out the BRI and recommend narrowing amendments. See MPEP §2111 for more on BRI. Use Form paragraphs 7.05/7.05.01 when making an eligibility rejection arising from Step 1 failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims whose BRI covers both statutory and non‑statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim's BRI embraces both statutory and non‑statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non‑statutory subject matter and fails Step 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 for failing to claim statutory subject matter. It is best practice for the examiner to point out the problematic BRI and recommend an amendment, if possible, to narrow the claim to statutory embodiments. Example: a 'computer readable medium' claim that can read as a compact disc (statutory) or a carrier wave (non‑statutory) is properly rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2A — directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: After finding a claim within a statutory category, determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 2A is the first part of the Alice/Mayo framework. If the claim as a whole is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) it is eligible at Pathway B and the eligibility analysis ends. If it is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES), further analysis at Step 2B is required to determine whether the claim amounts to 'significantly more' than the exception. Evaluate Step 2A after BRI and whole‑application review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A two‑prong inquiry — Prong One (recitation) vs Prong Two (integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong One: does the claim recite (set forth or describe) a judicial exception? Prong Two: if it recites an exception, do the additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Prong One as identification of whether the claim 'recites' an exception (either by explicitly setting it forth or by describing the concept). If Prong One is met, Prong Two examines whether additional claim elements transform/integrate the exception into a practical application so that the claim is not 'directed to' the exception. If additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and proceeds to Step 2B. See MPEP §2106.04(d)(2) for how to evaluate 'integration into a practical application.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — distinguish 'recites' from 'involves'
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim 'recites' an abstract idea/law of nature/natural phenomenon (i.e., sets it forth or describes it) rather than merely involving such a concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a claim stating 'elements that operate in accordance with F=ma' sets forth (recites) a law of nature and meets Prong One; a claim to a teeter‑totter (lever) merely involves the principle of mechanical advantage but does not recite it and thus does not meet Prong One. Examiners should identify specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an exception and then determine whether those limitations fall within the judicial exception categories. See MPEP §2106.04(a),(b),(c) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether additional elements in the claim integrate the recited judicial exception into a practical application; if so, the claim is not directed to the exception and is eligible at Pathway B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere inclusion of a judicial exception (e.g., a mathematical formula) means the claim 'recites' an exception, but does not necessarily make the claim 'directed to' it. Additional elements must do more than recite another judicial exception; they must transform the nature of the claim into a patent‑eligible application of the exception (Alice). If there are no additional elements (or if additional elements merely recite another judicial exception), the claim cannot be eligible on this basis and may require rejection and/or recommended amendment. See case examples (RecogniCorp, Genetic Techs.) and MPEP §2106.04(d)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling claims that recite multiple judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the same eligibility analysis regardless of how many judicial exceptions are recited; avoid parsing into multiple exceptions unless they are distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple distinct exceptions are present (e.g., one limitation is a law of nature and another is an abstract idea), examiners may select one exception and perform the analysis on that selected exception for efficiency. If analysis shows additional elements integrate or amount to significantly more than the selected exception, the claim is eligible. If multiple exceptions are not clearly distinct, treat them together as a single judicial exception for Prong Two and Step 2B. When possible, identify the claim as reciting the multiple types (e.g., mental steps + mathematical calculation) in the record to clarify analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea groupings (enumerated approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: To identify abstract ideas, use the Office's enumerated groupings: (1) mathematical concepts; (2) certain methods of organizing human activity; and (3) mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grouping approach distills relevant case law into clear categories for examination instead of relying solely on case comparisons. Examiners should (1) identify the specific claim limitation(s) believed to recite an abstract idea, and (2) determine whether those limitations fall within at least one grouping. If so, Prong One is satisfied and Prong Two analysis follows; if not, the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the abstract‑idea analysis concludes (except in rare circumstances). Note: software and business methods are not categorically excluded, and software is not automatically an abstract idea merely because it involves mathematical calculations. See MPEP §2106.04(a)(2) and cited cases (Enfish, McRO, Thales).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of the judicial exception does not avoid the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Even newly discovered or novel concepts (mathematical formulas, laws of nature, isolated natural products) can be judicial exceptions and thus excluded from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Flook, Mayo, Myriad) make clear that the novelty of the exception is not determinative for eligibility; a newly discovered law of nature or mathematical formula can still be an exception because allowing patents on such basic tools could preempt future innovation. Examiners should treat novel exceptions the same as long‑prevalent ones for the purposes of Step 2A/2B analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption is the underlying concern but not a standalone test
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusion of judicial exceptions is driven by concern over preemption, but preemption itself is not the test for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions of preemption should be addressed through application of the Alice/Mayo two‑part framework (Steps 2A and 2B). Absence of complete preemption does not automatically mean eligibility, and presence of preemption is resolved as part of the Alice/Mayo analysis. See cited cases (Mayo, Alice, Rapid Litigation Management).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure when claim fails Step 1 or Step 2A due to exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim fails Step 1 (not a statutory category) or fails Step 2A (directed to a judicial exception without integration), the examiner should make the appropriate 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection and follow form‑paragraph and best practice guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05 and 7.05.01) for Step 1 rejections. When a claim fails due to lack of additional elements integrating the exception, recommend amendments if possible that could resolve eligibility. If claim embraces non‑statutory embodiments but might be amended to statutory embodiments, proceed to analyze whether the amended claim would be eligible at Pathway A, B, or C and recommend amendments as a best practice.
